beats.visual: golden palace by the river Sarayu at dawn
beats.text: On the banks of the Sarayu stood Ayodhya, a city of peace and dharma, where no one ever went hungry.
Its king, Dasharatha, had wealth, power and his people's love. He had three queens. But he had no son.

beats.visual: the king alone on a moonlit balcony, worried
beats.text: Who would carry the line of the Sun after him? The question kept the old king awake.
On the advice of his guru, Sage Vasishtha, he invited the great sage Rishyasringa.
Together they performed the Putrakameshti Yagna, the sacred fire ritual for sons.

beats.visual: a divine being rising from the flames with a golden bowl of kheer
beats.text: From the fire rose a shining being, holding a golden bowl. 'Share this kheer among your queens,' he said.

beats.visual: old white-bearded King Dasharatha handing a golden bowl of kheer to his three queens Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra
beats.text: The king shared it between Kausalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi.
Soon, all three queens were with child. And so began the story that would shape the world.
In the month of Chaitra, on the ninth day, Queen Kaushalya gave birth to Rama, the embodiment of dharma. Today that day is celebrated as Ram Navami.

beats.visual: baby Rama glowing in a golden cradle
beats.text: Kaikeyi gave birth to Bharata. Sumitra gave birth to twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

beats.visual: four boys playing in the palace garden
beats.text: The four grew up inseparable. Lakshmana's heart belonged to Rama, and Shatrughna's to Bharata. Lakshmana would not even eat unless Rama was beside him.
Under Sage Vasishtha they mastered the Vedas, archery, riding elephants and chariots, and the duties of a righteous king.
Yet Rama was loved for more than his skill. Even as a boy he was kind to everyone, and he always spoke first, with a smile.

beats.visual: Dasharatha watching his sons with pride
beats.text: The old king looked at his four sons and felt that every one of his prayers had been answered. He did not know how soon the world would come asking for them.
Demons were destroying the prayers of the sages. Every time a sacrifice began, they rained blood and flesh on the sacred fire.
The great sage Vishwamitra came to Ayodhya for help. Dasharatha promised him anything he wished.
'Send Rama with me,' said the sage. Rama was not yet sixteen. Dasharatha was heartbroken, and offered his whole army instead.
But Vasishtha reminded him: a king's word cannot be broken. So Rama and Lakshmana went willingly.

beats.visual: princes walking behind the sage along the river
beats.text: On the road, Vishwamitra taught them the mantras Bala and Atibala, so they would never feel hunger, thirst or tiredness, and then the secrets of divine weapons.

beats.visual: Tataka charging out of the forest
beats.text: Then came Tataka, a fearsome demoness with the strength of a thousand elephants, who had turned a whole land into a wilderness.
Rama was reluctant to fight her, but the sage reminded him that a protector must protect the innocent. His arrow flew true, and the forest was free again.

beats.visual: sages at a yagna, fire glowing
beats.text: At Siddhashrama, where Lord Vishnu himself had once meditated, Vishwamitra began a sacred yagna in silence.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana standing guard at night
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana guarded it for six days and nights without sleep, bows always strung.
On the last day, the altar burst into flames and the sky went dark. The demon Subahu and his general Maricha came roaring down, ready to pour blood onto the fire.
Rama did not panic. He fitted the Manava astra to his bow.
It struck Maricha in the chest and hurled him a hundred yojanas, far across the ocean. Rama had chosen not to kill him.
Then the Agni astra struck Subahu, and he fell. With the Vayu astra, Rama swept the rest of the demons away.

beats.visual: Maricha alone on a distant shore, trembling
beats.text: But far away, Maricha woke up on a lonely shore, shaking. He would never forget that arrow.

title: Ahalya
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 48-49 (the stone form comes from later retellings)

beats.text: On the road to Mithila, they found an empty ashram, silent for centuries. No bird sang there.
'This was the home of Sage Gautama,' said Vishwamitra. 'His wife Ahalya was the most beautiful woman the creator ever made.'

beats.visual: Indra in disguise at the hermitage
beats.text: 'One day, Indra came disguised as Gautama, and Ahalya was deceived. When the sage returned, he cursed them both.'
'She would live here unseen, living on air, doing penance, until Rama came.' Many later tellings say she was turned to stone.
As Rama entered, the curse broke. Ahalya appeared, radiant and free, shining like the moon behind clouds.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana touching her feet
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana bowed and touched her feet, as one honors a mother.

beats.visual: Ahalya bowing, flowers falling from the sky
beats.text: She bowed in gratitude. Flowers fell from the sky, and divine drums sounded.
Rama had not fought anyone, yet he had won his gentlest victory. Her long penance had ended.
King Janaka of Mithila welcomed the princes with honor. He was a king and a sage at once, wise and gentle.

beats.visual: a giant bow on an iron cart pulled by many men
beats.text: In his palace lay Shiva's mighty bow, so heavy that it took hundreds of men to pull it on its eight-wheeled cart. Not even gods and demons could lift it.

beats.visual: kings failing to lift the bow
beats.text: Many kings had come for it. Not one could even raise it off the ground.
Janaka had made a vow: whoever strings this bow will marry my daughter, Sita.
Vishwamitra turned to Rama and smiled. He knew exactly why he had brought Rama here.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana looking at the bow in awe
beats.text: Rama looked at the bow and said quietly, 'May I touch it?' Janaka nodded, and the whole court held its breath.

beats.visual: the bow's box being opened, golden light
beats.text: Now the great box was opened. Rama stepped closer, and the whole hall fell silent.

title: The Birth of Sita
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 66 (the casket and the bow as a toy are from later retellings)

beats.visual: Janaka ploughing a field at sunrise
beats.text: Years earlier, King Janaka was ploughing a field himself to prepare the ground for a sacred ritual.

beats.visual: the plough striking something in the earth
beats.text: Suddenly, the plough struck something hard in the soil.

beats.visual: a golden casket rising from the furrow
beats.text: From the earth emerged a glowing baby girl. Some tellings say she lay in a golden casket.
Janaka lifted her in his arms. He had no child of his own, and his heart filled with joy.

beats.visual: the baby in the palace, flowers around her
beats.text: He named her Sita, meaning 'furrow.' Born of the Earth, she was raised as his own daughter, and loved by all of Mithila.

beats.visual: young Sita lifting the heavy bow with ease
beats.text: Later tellings say that as a girl, she once moved Shiva's bow aside like a toy while cleaning the room.
Janaka saw it and knew she was no ordinary child. Only a man who could string that same bow would be worthy of her.

title: The Swayamvar
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 67-73 (Ravana at the contest is from later retellings)

beats.text: Kings from across the land came to win Sita's hand. One by one, they failed. Some could not even move it.
In some later tellings, even mighty Ravana tried, and was crushed under the bow and left in shame.
Then Rama stepped forward. He bowed to his teacher, Vishwamitra, and walked to the bow.

beats.visual: Rama lifting the bow with one hand
beats.text: He lifted it as if it were light, and the whole court gasped.
As he drew the string to his ear, the bow broke in two, with a crack like thunder that shook Mithila. People fell to the ground in fear.
Janaka rose, tears in his eyes. 'My vow is fulfilled. Sita will marry Rama.'
She placed the garland around Rama's neck, and the sky rained flowers.
Their eyes met for a moment. Ancient tellings say they were Vishnu and Lakshmi, finding each other again on earth.

beats.visual: Janaka sending a message to Ayodhya
beats.text: Janaka sent swift messengers to Dasharatha with the happy news.
Dasharatha arrived with his whole court, his army and his sages. The two kings embraced like brothers.

beats.visual: Janaka with his daughters and nieces
beats.text: Janaka made a joyful offer: his daughters and his nieces for all four princes.
Sita to Rama, Urmila to Lakshmana. Janaka's brother Kushadhwaja's daughters, Mandavi and Shrutakirti, to Bharata and Shatrughna.
Four brothers married four sisters in one grand ceremony. They walked around the sacred fire together.

beats.visual: Sita and Rama at the fire
beats.text: As Janaka placed Sita's hand in Rama's, he said: 'She will follow you like your shadow.'
Flowers fell from the sky, and divine drums sounded.
His task complete, Vishwamitra blessed the couples and left for the Himalayas.
The whole city sang and danced for days. Janaka sent his daughters off with gold, silk, elephants and horses, and many tears.

beats.visual: the wedding procession on the road home
beats.text: On the way back to Ayodhya, a storm rose. The earth shook, and birds cried out.

beats.visual: Parashurama with his axe, eyes blazing
beats.text: A fearsome sage blocked the path. It was Parashurama, who had wiped out proud kings twenty-one times. His axe was on his shoulder.
Dasharatha begged him to spare his sons. Parashurama ignored him.
'You broke Shiva's bow,' he said to Rama. 'Now string Vishnu's bow, if you can.'
Rama took the bow, strung it, and fixed an arrow in one smooth motion.
'This arrow cannot go to waste,' said Rama. 'Shall I destroy your path, or the worlds you have won by your penance?'
Parashurama recognized the truth. He bowed, gave up his worlds to the arrow, and withdrew in peace.

beats.visual: Parashurama's eyes softening as he recognizes Vishnu
beats.text: Looking into Rama's eyes, Parashurama saw Lord Vishnu himself, and his anger melted away.

title: The Coronation Plan
onscreen: Tomorrow, a king would be crowned…

beats.text: For twelve years, Ayodhya was happy under Dasharatha. Rama and Sita lived in joy, and the people adored their eldest prince.
He called his ministers and the kings of the land. 'I have served long enough,' he said. 'I wish to crown Rama as Yuvaraja, the heir to the throne.'
The whole court roared its approval. 'Rama is truthful, brave and kind,' they said. 'Crown him!'
Vasishtha fixed the ceremony for the very next morning, under the star Pushya. Bharata and Shatrughna were away at their uncle's kingdom.
News spread, and the city burst into celebration. Streets were sprinkled with water, flags flew from every roof, and lamps were lit through the night.
Only Rama stayed quiet and humble. He never wanted the throne. He wanted only to serve.

beats.visual: Manthara on the palace roof watching the celebration
beats.text: From a palace terrace, a hunchbacked maid named Manthara watched the flags and flowers with a sour face.

beats.visual: Manthara asking why the city celebrates
beats.text: 'Why is the city rejoicing?' she asked. When she heard Rama would be crowned, she burned with anger and ran to her queen.
'Wake up, foolish queen! Rama becomes king tomorrow, and your son Bharata will be nothing. A servant to Rama for life.'

beats.visual: Kaikeyi giving Manthara a jewel in joy
beats.text: But Kaikeyi was delighted. She gave Manthara a jewel. 'Rama is like my own son,' she said.
Manthara threw it away. 'Remember the two boons the king once gave you, when you saved his life in the war against the demons?'
At first Kaikeyi loved Rama as her own son. But slowly, the poison of doubt took hold.

beats.visual: Kaikeyi removing her jewels, lying on the floor
beats.text: She tore off her jewels, put on soiled clothes, and lay on the bare floor of the anger chamber.
Dasharatha came looking for his favorite queen, and found her on the floor of the dark chamber, her hair loose and her jewels scattered.
'Who has hurt you?' he cried. 'Ask anything, and I swear by Rama, whom I love more than my life, I will give it.'
Kaikeyi rose. 'Two boons you promised me long ago. First: Bharata becomes king. Second: Rama goes to the forest for fourteen years, dressed as a hermit.'
The king fell to the ground as if struck by lightning. He begged, wept and pleaded. He even touched her feet.
'You are the king of the Ikshvaku line,' she said coldly. 'Will you break your word?' Kaikeyi did not move.

beats.visual: night passing, the king awake in grief
beats.text: The whole night passed. The king lay awake, calling Rama's name, praying that the dawn would never come.
A king bound by his word. A father bound by love.

title: Rama Accepts Exile
onscreen: The kingdom lost. The dharma kept.

beats.visual: Rama arriving at the palace at dawn
beats.text: At dawn, Rama came to greet his father, expecting a blessing for his coronation. He found him broken, unable even to speak.
'What has happened, mother?' asked Rama. 'Have I displeased my father?'
Kaikeyi told him everything: the two boons, the throne for Bharata, the forest for him.
Rama did not argue or frown. 'If my father's word needs it, I go gladly,' he said. 'Why would I need the crown when I have his honor?'
He went to his mother Kaushalya. She fainted with grief, and begged to come with him.

beats.visual: Lakshmana in fury, hand on his sword
beats.text: Lakshmana raged and wanted to fight for the throne. Rama calmed him. 'This is destiny,' he said. 'No one is to blame.'

beats.visual: Rama removing his royal robes, putting on bark cloth
beats.text: Rama took off his silk and jewels and put on clothes of tree bark.

beats.visual: Rama walking away from the throne
beats.text: He gave up a kingdom as easily as one lets go of a flower.
Rama asked Sita to stay behind. 'The forest is hard and dangerous. There are snakes, wild beasts, thorns and demons.'
'Where you are is my home,' she said. 'Even a palace without you is a jungle. With you, the forest will be a garden.'
When Rama still refused, she wept and declared she would die rather than be left behind. At last, Rama agreed.
Lakshmana too refused to be left behind. 'I will walk ahead of you with my bow,' he said. 'I will serve you day and night.'
His mother Sumitra blessed him: 'Think of Rama as your father, Sita as your mother, and the forest as Ayodhya.'

beats.visual: three figures leaving the palace gate
beats.text: The three left Ayodhya in bark cloth, in the chariot of the minister Sumantra.

beats.visual: the whole city following in tears
beats.text: The whole city followed them in tears, running behind the chariot.

beats.visual: old Dasharatha falling in the dust
beats.text: Behind them, the old king fell in the dust, watching until the chariot was gone.

title: Guha and the Ganga
source: Valmiki, Ayodhya Kanda 46-52 (Kevat washing Rama's feet is from the Ramcharitmanas)

beats.visual: Rama leaving the sleeping citizens behind at night
beats.text: The people of Ayodhya would not turn back, so Rama left quietly at night while they slept.

beats.visual: a wide river at dawn, a boatman waiting
beats.text: At the Ganga, the boatman king Guha of Shringaverapura welcomed Rama as a dear friend.

beats.visual: Guha offering food and his kingdom
beats.text: He brought food and offered his whole kingdom. Rama refused gently. He had a vow to keep: no royal comforts for fourteen years.
Later tellings say the boatman washed Rama's feet before letting him in the boat, in case his touch turned the boat into a woman, as it had Ahalya.
Rama sent the minister Sumantra home with the empty chariot and a message of love for his father.
Guha rowed them across. Sita folded her hands and prayed to the Ganga for their safe return.

beats.visual: Rama cutting his hair into a sage's matted locks
beats.text: On the far bank, Rama and Lakshmana matted their hair with the sap of a banyan tree.

beats.visual: Rama dressed as a forest sage
beats.text: Here Rama gave up the last sign of royalty and became a forest sage.

title: Dasharatha's Death
onscreen: A father who died of love.

beats.text: With Rama gone, Ayodhya lost its light. No fires were lit, no songs were sung, and the markets were empty.

beats.visual: Sumantra returning with the empty chariot
beats.text: When Sumantra returned with the empty chariot, the king fainted.
Dasharatha cried Rama's name day and night. Then he remembered a curse from long ago.

beats.visual: young Dasharatha hunting by a river at night
beats.text: As a young prince, he had shot an arrow at a sound in the dark, thinking it was an elephant drinking.

beats.visual: the dying hermit boy with a water pot
beats.text: It was a young hermit filling a pot of water for his blind parents. Later tellings call him Shravan Kumar.

beats.visual: the old blind parents of the hermit
beats.text: The grieving parents cursed him: 'You too will die of grief, separated from your son.'

beats.visual: the king whispering in his last breath
beats.text: Now the curse had come true. On the sixth night, at midnight, he whispered, 'Rama, Rama,' and was gone.
At dawn, the queens found him still. The whole palace broke into cries.
Far away in his uncle's kingdom, Bharata had a terrible dream about his father.

beats.visual: Bharata riding home from his uncle's kingdom
beats.text: Bharata was away when all this happened. Messengers called him home in haste, without telling him why.
He felt something was wrong the moment he saw the silent city. No one greeted him. No one smiled.
Kaikeyi proudly told him: 'Your father is gone. Rama is in exile. The throne is yours.'
Bharata was shattered. 'You have destroyed my family for my sake? You are no mother of mine! I want nothing of this.'
He ran to Kaushalya, fell at her feet and swore he had known nothing of the plot.
He performed his father's last rites with Shatrughna, weeping beside the funeral fire.
When the ministers offered him the crown, he refused it. He set out to bring his brother home.

beats.visual: Bharata and the whole city marching into the forest
beats.text: Bharata led an army of citizens, queens and sages into the forest to find Rama.

beats.visual: Lakshmana seeing the army from a tree
beats.text: Seeing the army, Lakshmana thought Bharata had come to attack, and raised his bow. Rama stopped him. 'Bharata would never harm us.'
At Chitrakoot, Bharata found Rama's small hut. He fell at Rama's feet, weeping. 'Return and rule, brother.'

beats.visual: Rama learning of his father's death
beats.text: Then Rama learned that his father was dead. He wept, and offered water to his father's spirit at the river.
Rama embraced Bharata. 'Our father gave his word. I must keep it, and you must rule.'
Bharata would not give in. He sat outside the hut and vowed to fast until Rama agreed.

beats.visual: the sages watching the two brothers
beats.text: For hours, two brothers each tried to give the kingdom to the other. The sages watching had never seen such a contest.

beats.visual: the two brothers sitting face to face
beats.text: Neither would take the throne. Each only wanted the other to have it.
At last, Bharata asked for one thing. 'Give me your sandals.'

beats.visual: Rama placing his sandals in Bharata's hands
beats.text: Rama agreed. He stepped onto a pair of golden sandals and gave them to his brother.

beats.visual: Bharata carrying the sandals on his head
beats.text: Bharata carried them on his head all the way home, as if he were carrying Rama himself.
'If you do not return on the very day the fourteen years end,' he said, 'I will enter the fire.'

beats.visual: the sandals on the throne of Ayodhya
beats.text: He placed them on the throne and ruled in Rama's name, as a servant. Every decision was first laid before the sandals.

beats.visual: Bharata living in a simple hut at Nandigram
beats.text: He would not live in the palace. He lived in a simple hut at Nandigram, outside the city, wearing bark cloth and matted hair.
He lived like an ascetic for fourteen years, waiting for his brother.

beats.visual: Rama leaving Chitrakoot for the deeper forest
beats.text: And Rama, so that the people would stop coming, went deeper into the forest.

title: Atri and Anasuya
onscreen: A blessing for what was to come.

beats.visual: a peaceful forest hermitage by a stream
beats.text: Deep in the forest, they visited the ashram of Sage Atri, one of the seven great sages of the universe.
Atri welcomed them like his own children, and led Sita to meet his wife.

beats.visual: Anasuya, an aged woman glowing with spiritual power
beats.text: Anasuya was very old, her hair white, her body thin from penance. Once, her prayers had made the Ganga flow through a land dying of drought, and had stopped ten years of famine.
Atri's wife, Anasuya, a woman of great virtue, embraced Sita like a daughter.

beats.visual: Anasuya giving Sita jewels and a garland
beats.text: She was so pleased with Sita's devotion to Rama that she gave her divine gifts: a garland that never withers, clothes that never fade, and an ointment that would keep her beautiful forever.
She spoke to Sita about devotion and strength, wisdom Sita would need in the days ahead.

beats.visual: the three walking on at dawn
beats.text: The next morning, the three walked on into the Dandaka forest, wearing those gifts.

title: Viradha
onscreen: The first demon. Not the last.

beats.visual: the sages of Dandaka welcoming Rama
beats.text: At the edge of the Dandaka forest, the sages welcomed Rama with fruit and flowers. 'Protect us,' they begged. 'Demons hunt us here.'
As they moved deeper into the forest, a terrible demon, Viradha, rose before them. He was as tall as a mountain, with a gaping mouth, wearing a tiger's skin dripping with blood.
He snatched Sita and mocked the princes. 'You wear the clothes of hermits, but carry bows and a woman. I will make her my wife.'
Rama and Lakshmana's arrows struck again and again, but the demon could not be killed by weapons. He had a boon from Brahma.
So the brothers broke his arms and wrestled him to the ground.

beats.visual: the princes burying him in a pit
beats.text: At last, they buried him alive in a deep pit. Before dying, he revealed he was a cursed celestial named Tumburu, now free.
For ten years, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana wandered from ashram to ashram. Then they met the great Sage Agastya.
He guided them to Panchavati, a lovely land beside the Godavari river.

beats.visual: a beautiful riverside grove with five banyan trees
beats.text: It was named for its five great banyan trees. Lotus ponds shone, and peacocks danced on the banks.

beats.visual: Jatayu meeting them on the way
beats.text: On the way, they met an old vulture, Jatayu, who said he was a friend of their father. 'I will guard Sita when you are away,' he promised.
Lakshmana built a simple cottage of leaves and bamboo, with clay walls and a floor of sacred grass.

beats.visual: the three sitting by the river at sunset
beats.text: For a while, they lived in peace. Deer came close. Birds sang at dawn. Winter came, and Rama and Lakshmana bathed in the cold river at first light.
These were the happiest days of their exile. But a storm was already on its way.

title: Surpanakha
onscreen: An insult that would burn Lanka.

beats.visual: a demoness watching Rama from the trees
beats.text: One day, Ravana's sister Surpanakha saw Rama and fell in love. She had a pot belly, copper-colored hair and long claws for nails.

beats.visual: her turning into a beautiful woman
beats.text: She took a beautiful form and asked him to marry her. 'Leave this thin woman,' she said. 'I will eat her, and we will wander the forest together.'
Rama smiled and said, 'I am married. Ask my brother. He is alone here.'
Lakshmana laughed and refused too. 'I am only a servant. Go back to Rama. He will make you his second wife.'
She realized they were mocking her. Her beautiful form fell away, and her true face burned with rage.
Furious, she lunged at Sita, her claws reaching for her throat.
Lakshmana struck first and cut off her nose and ears.
Bleeding and burning with hatred, she fled through the forest, howling, to her brothers.
Surpanakha fell bleeding at the feet of her brother Khara, ruler of the demons in Janasthana, and begged for revenge.
Khara sent fourteen fierce warriors to kill Rama. Rama killed all of them with fourteen arrows.

beats.visual: a vast demon army, thousands strong
beats.text: Then Khara and his general Dushana brought fourteen thousand demons to the forest, with chariots, elephants and weapons of every kind.

beats.visual: evil omens: blood rain, jackals howling
beats.text: Evil omens filled the sky. Blood fell like rain, and jackals howled at noon. But Khara would not turn back.

beats.visual: Rama sending Sita and Lakshmana to a cave
beats.text: Rama sent Sita and Lakshmana to a cave in the mountain. 'This fight is mine,' he said.
He faced the whole army alone, wearing armor that shone like the sun. His arrows filled the sky.
Dushana fell. Then the three-headed Trishira. Then, at last, Khara himself.
By evening, the entire army lay still. The sages came out of hiding and showered Rama with flowers.
In golden Lanka, the ten-headed king Ravana sat on his throne, among his ministers.

beats.visual: Surpanakha before Ravana in his court
beats.text: Surpanakha burst into the court and showed her wounds to Ravana. 'You sit here drinking while a man destroys your army!'
She described Sita's beauty and goaded him. 'Take her, and destroy Rama. She should be your queen.'

beats.visual: Ravana's flying chariot crossing the sea
beats.text: Ravana flew across the ocean in his golden flying chariot, pulled by donkeys with demon faces.
He went to Maricha, the demon Rama had once thrown across the ocean, now living as a hermit.
'Do not touch Rama,' Maricha begged. 'I have felt his arrow. Every tree in this forest looks like Rama to me.'

beats.visual: Ravana threatening Maricha with his sword
beats.text: But Ravana drew his sword. 'Help me, or die by my hand right now.'
Maricha agreed. 'If I go, Rama will kill me. If I stay, you will. Better to die by Rama's hand.'
Together they flew toward Panchavati.

beats.visual: a shimmering golden deer near the hut
beats.text: One morning, Sita saw a deer with a golden coat and silver spots. Its horns shone like jewels, and its hooves were like blue sapphire.
It played near the hut, coming close, then running away, as if it wanted to be seen.
Sita was enchanted. 'Rama, please catch it for me! If it lives, we will take it home to Ayodhya. If not, its golden skin will be a seat.'
Lakshmana was uneasy. 'Brother, no deer like this exists. It could be a demon's trick. It could be Maricha.'
But Rama could not refuse Sita. 'If it is Maricha, I will kill him,' he said.
'Guard her well,' he told Lakshmana. 'Do not leave her alone for a moment.'

beats.visual: Rama following the deer into the forest
beats.text: And he followed the deer into the forest.

beats.visual: the deer leading him far away
beats.text: The deer led him deeper and deeper, appearing and vanishing among the trees, far away from the hut.

title: The Lakshman Rekha
onscreen: The line that must not be crossed.
source: Valmiki, Aranya Kanda 44-45 (the drawn line comes from later retellings)

beats.text: Far away, Rama's arrow hit the deer, and it turned back into Maricha, a giant demon falling to the ground.
With his dying breath, he cried out in Rama's voice: 'Sita! Lakshmana! Help me!'

beats.visual: Rama realizing the trick, running back
beats.text: Rama understood the trick at once, and began to run back toward the hut.
At the hut, Sita heard the cry and begged Lakshmana to go. He refused. 'No one in the three worlds can harm Rama.'

beats.visual: Sita speaking harsh words in fear
beats.text: Mad with fear, she spoke harsh words. She accused him of wanting Rama dead. Lakshmana covered his ears.

beats.visual: Lakshmana drawing a line around the hut
beats.text: Hurt but obedient, he drew a line around the hut, as later tellings say. 'Do not cross this, whatever happens.'

beats.visual: Lakshmana praying to the forest spirits
beats.text: He bowed to the trees and the forest spirits, and asked them to protect her.
Then he went to find his brother, looking back again and again.

beats.visual: a sage at the door, begging
beats.text: As soon as he left, an old sage with an umbrella and a water pot came to the hut, asking for alms.
The trees stopped moving. The river grew still. Even the wind was afraid.
Sita saw nothing wrong with the old man. She offered him food and water from inside the line, as later tellings say.

beats.visual: the sage refusing, demanding she step out
beats.text: He insisted she come out. 'A holy man cannot take alms from behind a line.' She stepped over the line.

beats.visual: the sage revealing ten heads, Ravana
beats.text: The sage turned into Ravana, king of Lanka, his ten heads blazing with anger.
'Be my queen,' he said, 'and rule golden Lanka.' Sita refused. 'You are a jackal. Rama is a lion.'
He seized her and flew into the sky in his golden chariot.

beats.visual: Sita crying out to the trees and river
beats.text: 'Tell Rama!' she cried to the trees, the river and the deer. Sita's cries echoed across the forest.

title: Jatayu
onscreen: A bird who gave his life for dharma.

beats.visual: the great vulture on a tree
beats.text: Jatayu, an old vulture and friend of Dasharatha, heard Sita's cries.
'I am sixty thousand years old,' he called, 'but I will not let you take her. Put her down, Ravana!'
Though weak with age, he attacked Ravana with all his strength.
He broke the chariot, killed the donkeys and the charioteer, and wounded the demon king with his claws.
But Ravana drew his sword and cut off the old bird's wings. Jatayu fell.

beats.visual: Sita's jewels falling from the sky
beats.text: As Ravana flew on, Sita dropped her jewels, wrapped in her scarf, onto a mountain where five monkeys sat.
Later, Rama and Lakshmana found the dying bird. He lived long enough to tell Rama everything.
'Ravana took her south,' he whispered, and died in Rama's arms.
Rama performed his funeral like a son, and wept for him as he had for his father.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana searching the forest
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana searched everywhere for Sita, calling her name through forests and mountains. Rama asked the trees, the rivers and the deer if they had seen her.

beats.visual: a huge headless demon with long arms
beats.text: Suddenly, a giant demon named Kabandha seized them in his arms. He had no head or neck. His mouth was in his belly, and a single fiery eye glowed in his chest.

beats.visual: the brothers cutting off his arms
beats.text: Rama cut off the right arm, Lakshmana the left. Kabandha crashed to the ground and cried out in relief.
'I was a celestial named Danu,' he said. 'Indra struck me with his thunderbolt and drove my head into my body. Only you could free me.'

beats.visual: a radiant being rising from the funeral fire
beats.text: The brothers burned his body on a great fire. From the flames rose a radiant being, shining in a celestial chariot.

beats.visual: the celestial pointing toward a mountain
beats.text: He gave them a clue: 'Seek Sugriva, king of the monkeys, at Mount Rishyamukha. He knows Ravana's way. And first, visit Shabari.'

title: Shabari
source: Valmiki, Aranya Kanda 74 (the tasted berries come from later retellings)

beats.visual: an old woman sweeping a forest path
beats.text: Near Lake Pampa lived Shabari, an aged devotee who had waited years for Rama. She was a tribal woman, born far from any palace.

beats.visual: Shabari as a young girl leaving home
beats.text: As a young girl, she had run away from home to serve the sage Matanga. Before he died, he told her: 'Wait here. One day, Rama will come.'

beats.visual: Shabari carrying a basket of berries
beats.text: Each day she gathered the sweetest berries, tasting each one to be sure it was good, as later tellings lovingly say.
And one day, two princes walked up the path. Shabari fell at Rama's feet, weeping.

beats.visual: Rama eating the berries with joy
beats.text: When Rama finally came, he happily ate the berries she had already tasted. Lakshmana hesitated. Rama did not.
He cared nothing for rank or custom. He saw only her love.

beats.visual: Shabari rising into the sky in light
beats.text: Shabari told them where to find Sugriva. Then, her life's wish fulfilled, she entered a sacred fire and rose to heaven.

beats.visual: Sugriva watching from a mountain, afraid
beats.text: On Rishyamukha, the exiled monkey king Sugriva saw two warriors approaching with bows. He feared his brother Vali had sent them to kill him.
So he sent his wisest minister, Hanuman, son of the wind god, to find out who they were.

beats.visual: Hanuman disguised as a humble brahmin
beats.text: Hanuman came disguised as a priest. He spoke so wisely and gently that Rama turned to Lakshmana in wonder.
'He has spoken for so long, without a single mistake,' Rama said. 'Only one who has mastered the Vedas could speak like this.'
Lakshmana told him everything: the exile, Sita, and Ravana.

beats.visual: Hanuman revealing his true form, bowing
beats.text: Hanuman revealed his true form and fell at Rama's feet, knowing instantly who he was. His heart overflowed.

beats.visual: Hanuman lifting both brothers on his shoulders
beats.text: He grew large, lifted both brothers on his shoulders, and leapt up the mountain.
He carried them to Sugriva. A lifelong devotion had begun. From that day, Hanuman lived only for Rama.

beats.visual: Rama and Sugriva before a sacred fire
beats.text: Hanuman lit a sacred fire. Rama and Sugriva walked around it together and sealed their friendship. 'Your joy is my joy,' Rama said. 'Your sorrow is my sorrow.'
Sugriva told his story. His brother Vali, king of Kishkindha, had driven him out, taken his kingdom and his wife Ruma.

beats.visual: Vali fighting a demon in a cave, flashback
beats.text: Once, Vali had chased a demon into a cave, and Sugriva waited outside for a year. When blood flowed out, he thought Vali was dead, and sealed the cave.
But Vali returned alive, and never forgave him. 'Help me,' Sugriva said, 'and my army will find Sita.'
Rama promised to defeat Vali.
Then Sugriva showed him the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away, wrapped in her yellow scarf.
Lakshmana said: 'I do not know her earrings or bracelets. I only ever looked at her feet. These anklets are hers.'

title: The Fall of Vali
source: Valmiki, Kishkindha Kanda 11-26 (Vali's boon to take half his enemy's strength comes from later retellings)

beats.visual: Rama splitting seven sal trees with one arrow
beats.text: To prove his strength, Rama shot one arrow through seven giant sal trees, and it came back to his quiver.

beats.visual: Sugriva challenging Vali at his gate
beats.text: Sugriva challenged Vali to a duel. Vali, the mightiest monkey, was said to take half the strength of any enemy who faced him.
The two looked alike, and Rama hesitated to shoot, fearing he might hit the wrong one. Sugriva fled, bleeding.

beats.visual: Sugriva wearing a garland as a mark
beats.text: The next day, Sugriva wore a garland of flowers as a mark.
Vali's wife Tara begged him not to fight. 'Sugriva has a new ally. Rama.' Vali did not listen.

beats.visual: Rama's arrow flying from behind a tree
beats.text: This time Rama's arrow flew true from behind a tree, and Vali fell.
Vali asked, 'Why strike from hiding?' Rama explained his duty: Vali had taken his brother's wife, and a king must punish that.
Vali accepted, and asked Rama to protect his son, Angada. Sugriva was crowned king of Kishkindha.
With the monsoon season, no army could march. Rama and Lakshmana waited in a cave on Mount Prasravana for four long months.

beats.visual: rivers flooding, lightning over the forest
beats.text: Rivers flooded, lightning cracked over the forest, and the roads disappeared under water.

beats.visual: Rama gazing at the sky, alone
beats.text: Every night, Rama grieved for Sita. The storms only made it harder. Every peacock's cry, every flash of lightning reminded him of her.
Lakshmana sat beside him. 'Grief steals strength,' he said. 'Hold on, brother. We will find her.'

beats.visual: Sugriva enjoying luxury in his palace
beats.text: Meanwhile, Sugriva fell into comfort, with music, wine and his queens, and forgot his promise.

beats.visual: the rains ending, clear autumn sky
beats.text: Autumn came. The sky cleared. But no army gathered.

beats.visual: Lakshmana storming into the city, bow in hand
beats.text: When the rains ended, an angry Lakshmana came to remind him. He twanged his bow, and the whole city shook.
Wise Queen Tara came out first and calmed him. Sugriva was ashamed, and ordered every monkey army in the world to gather.

beats.visual: monkey armies arriving from every direction
beats.text: Millions of monkeys and bears came from mountains, forests and oceans, covering the land like clouds.

beats.visual: monkey armies leaving in four directions
beats.text: Sugriva sent search parties to the east, west, north and south. 'Come back within one month,' he ordered, 'or face death.'
Rama gave Hanuman his signet ring, engraved with his name. 'Show this to Sita. She will know you come from me.'

beats.visual: the southern party led by Angada, Jambavan and Hanuman
beats.text: The southern party, led by Prince Angada, with Jambavan and Hanuman, searched cave after cave.

beats.visual: the monkeys trapped in a magical cave
beats.text: They wandered into a magical underground cave and were lost there, until a holy woman, Swayamprabha, brought them out with her power.

beats.visual: monkeys sitting hopelessly on a beach
beats.text: When they came out, they were on the shore of the southern ocean. A month had passed. They had found nothing.

beats.visual: Angada declaring he will fast to death
beats.text: The deadline was gone. Despair settled in. Angada sat down to fast until death, rather than return in shame.

beats.visual: the monkeys sitting in silence by the sea
beats.text: One by one, the others sat beside him, facing the endless sea.

beats.visual: the great vulture Sampati, wingless on a cliff
beats.text: On the shore, a huge old vulture crawled out of a cave. It was Sampati, brother of the fallen Jatayu. He had no wings.
At first he was glad. 'Food has come to me,' he said. Then he heard them speak of Jatayu's death, and he cried out.
Long ago, he and Jatayu had raced toward the sun. Sampati spread his wings to shield his brother, and the sun burned them away.
With his sharp vulture eyes he saw far across the ocean. 'I see Lanka,' he said, 'and a woman weeping in a garden.'

beats.visual: the monkeys staring at the endless sea
beats.text: Lanka was a hundred yojanas away across the water. One said he could jump ten. Another, fifty. Angada could jump the distance, but not return.
Jambavan, the wise old bear, knew who could.
He turned to Hanuman, who sat alone, saying nothing.

beats.visual: baby Hanuman leaping at the sun
beats.text: As a baby, Hanuman thought the rising sun was a ripe fruit, and leapt into the sky to eat it.

beats.visual: Indra striking him with a thunderbolt
beats.text: Indra struck him with his thunderbolt, and he fell. The gods blessed him with great powers.

beats.visual: Hanuman sitting alone, forgetting his powers
beats.text: But as a child, a curse from the sages had made Hanuman forget his own strength, until someone reminded him.
Jambavan spoke of his birth, his speed and his courage. 'You are the son of the wind. Rise, Hanuman. The whole world waits for you.'
Slowly, Hanuman remembered. His body began to glow.

beats.visual: Hanuman growing to a mountain's size
beats.text: He grew vast as a mountain and stood on Mount Mahendra. The earth trembled. Rocks cracked. Animals ran from their caves.

beats.visual: Hanuman bowing to the gods before the leap
beats.text: He bowed to the sun, to Indra, to the wind, and to Rama.
'Jai Shri Ram!' he roared, and leapt toward Lanka. The mountain sank under the force, and trees flew after him into the sky.
Hanuman flew over the ocean like a comet. The ocean god raised the golden mountain Mainaka from the waves to let him rest.

beats.visual: Hanuman touching the mountain and flying on
beats.text: Hanuman only touched it with his hand in thanks. 'I cannot rest until I find Sita,' he said.

beats.visual: the sea-serpent Surasa rising with a huge open mouth
beats.text: The gods tested Hanuman on his flight. First, the sea-serpent Surasa rose with a huge open mouth. 'No one passes without entering my mouth.'

beats.visual: Hanuman growing larger, Surasa's mouth growing
beats.text: Hanuman grew larger, and her mouth grew larger. Ten yojanas. Twenty. Ninety.

beats.visual: Hanuman shrinking to a thumb's size
beats.text: Then he shrank to the size of a thumb, flew in and slipped out through her jaws. She smiled and blessed him.

beats.visual: the shadow-demoness Simhika reaching up from the water
beats.text: Next, Simhika, a demoness who caught creatures by their shadows, grabbed his shadow and dragged him down.
Hanuman let himself fall into her mouth, entered her body and tore free.

beats.visual: Hanuman flying on over the calm sea
beats.text: The sea was clear. Ahead, on the horizon, golden Lanka began to shine.

beats.visual: golden Lanka glowing on the horizon
beats.text: At last Hanuman landed on Mount Lamba in Lanka, a city of gold with towering walls, built on a mountain peak in the middle of the sea.
Its walls were gold, its gates were guarded by thousands of demons with spears and bows, and its moats were full of crocodiles.

beats.visual: Hanuman shrinking to the size of a cat
beats.text: So he waited for night. Then he shrank to the size of a cat and crept toward the gate in the moonlight.

beats.visual: Lankini, the guardian demoness, blocking him
beats.text: Lankini, the guardian spirit of the city, stopped him. She was huge and terrible, with blazing eyes. 'No one enters Lanka,' she roared, 'without my permission.'

beats.visual: Hanuman striking her once with his left hand
beats.text: Hanuman did not want to kill a woman. He struck her lightly, just once, with his left fist.
She fell, and remembered Brahma's old prophecy: 'When a monkey defeats you, Lanka's end is near.'
'Go in, mighty one,' she said, 'and find the daughter of Janaka.'

beats.visual: Hanuman searching Ravana's palace at night
beats.text: Hanuman searched Ravana's palace room by room, past drunken guards, dancing halls and golden chambers, but found no Sita.

beats.visual: Hanuman seeing Ravana asleep among his queens
beats.text: He saw Ravana asleep, surrounded by beautiful queens. For a moment he thought one was Sita, then shook his head. 'Sita would never sleep here, happy.'

beats.visual: Hanuman sitting in despair on a wall
beats.text: He searched every house in Lanka. Nothing. He sat on a wall in despair. Had she died? Had he failed Rama?

beats.visual: Hanuman gazing at a garden of Ashoka trees
beats.text: At last he saw a garden of Ashoka trees, glowing in the moonlight.

beats.visual: a thin, pale woman in plain clothes under a tree
beats.text: Beneath one tree sat a thin, pale woman in plain, dusty yellow clothes, her hair in a single braid, her eyes full of tears.
Ferocious demonesses guarded her, with the faces of horses, boars and buffaloes. She wept, whispering Rama's name.

beats.visual: Hanuman hiding in the tree above
beats.text: Hanuman hid in the branches above, his heart pounding. He had found her.

beats.visual: Ravana arriving in the garden at dawn with his queens
beats.text: At dawn, Ravana came to the garden, surrounded by his queens and torchbearers, with music playing.

beats.visual: Ravana threatening Sita in the garden
beats.text: 'Marry me,' he said, 'and all of Lanka is yours.' When she refused, he roared: 'Then in two months I will have you cut up for my breakfast.'
Sita placed a blade of grass between them and refused to even look at him. 'Rama will come, and you will die.'
Ravana stormed away. The demonesses taunted her until she was alone.
Then an old demoness, Trijata, woke up shaking. 'I dreamed that Rama came on a white elephant, and Lanka sank into the sea. Do not harm her.'

beats.visual: Hanuman softly singing Rama's story from the tree
beats.text: Then a gentle voice from the tree began to sing the story of Rama: Ayodhya, the exile, the golden deer, the search.
Sita looked up and saw a small monkey among the leaves, his hands folded.

title: The Ring and the Jewel
onscreen: A message. A jewel. A hope.

beats.visual: Sita afraid it is a trick
beats.text: At first, Sita was afraid. Was this Ravana in disguise again?

beats.visual: Hanuman dropping Rama's ring into Sita's hands
beats.text: Hanuman climbed down, bowed, and dropped Rama's ring into her lap. She saw Rama's name on it and wept with joy, as if she had seen Rama himself.
He told her how Rama could not sleep or eat, and spoke her name every night.

beats.visual: Hanuman offering to carry her away
beats.text: He offered to carry her back right then, on his back, across the ocean.
'No,' said Sita. 'Rama must come and rescue me himself, for his honor. And I will not willingly touch another man.'

beats.visual: Sita telling the story of the crow
beats.text: She told him a secret only Rama knew: how Rama once punished a crow that hurt her with a single blade of grass, made into a divine weapon.

beats.visual: Sita giving her jewel, the Choodamani
beats.text: She gave him her hair jewel, the Choodamani, as proof. 'Tell Rama I am waiting. I can live one month more.'
Before leaving, Hanuman wanted to test Ravana's strength. He tore through the palace garden, uprooting trees and smashing pavilions.

beats.visual: Hanuman fighting the guards and Akshayakumara
beats.text: Guards came and fell. Eighty thousand of them. Then Ravana's own young son Akshayakumara fell too.
Ravana sent his greatest son, Indrajit. Hanuman allowed Indrajit's Brahmastra to bind him, so he could meet Ravana.
He was dragged before Ravana. Hanuman made a seat of his own tail, coiled higher than the king's throne.
He warned him: 'Return Sita, or face Rama. Not even the gods can save you from his arrows.'

beats.visual: Ravana ordering death, Vibhishana stopping him
beats.text: Ravana ordered his death, but his brother Vibhishana stopped him. 'A messenger must not be killed.'

beats.visual: a burning tail, Hanuman leaping over rooftops
beats.text: So Ravana ordered his tail set on fire. Hanuman shrank, broke free, and leapt from roof to roof.
He burned Lanka to the ground, sparing only the Ashoka grove where Sita sat. Then he dipped his tail in the sea.

beats.visual: Hanuman flying back over the ocean
beats.text: Hanuman flew back over the ocean and landed on Mahendra mountain with a roar, where the monkeys cheered his return.
On the way home they celebrated in Sugriva's honey garden, Madhuvana, eating and drinking until the guards complained.
When Sugriva heard, he smiled. 'They would only dare to do this if they had found Sita.'
Hanuman knelt before Rama and told him everything. 'I have seen Sita. She is alive and faithful.'
He placed her jewel in Rama's hands.

beats.visual: Rama holding the jewel to his heart
beats.text: Rama held it to his heart and wept. He remembered the day Janaka gave it to Sita at their wedding.
'I have nothing to give you, Hanuman, but this embrace,' said Rama, and held him close.
Then Rama rose. 'We march to the ocean. Now.'

beats.visual: millions of monkeys and bears marching
beats.text: Sugriva's army set out for the southern shore, millions strong. Monkeys and bears covered the mountains like a moving forest.

beats.visual: Hanuman carrying Rama, Angada carrying Lakshmana
beats.text: Hanuman carried Rama on his shoulders, and Angada carried Lakshmana.

beats.visual: the army eating fruit, crossing rivers
beats.text: They ate fruit and honey from the forests, crossed rivers and mountains, and never stopped to rest.
They reached the sea and stopped. The waves were endless. How could an army cross such water?

beats.visual: Rama looking across the sea toward Lanka
beats.text: Rama stood on the shore, looking south toward Lanka, where Sita waited.

beats.visual: Rama sitting in prayer on the shore
beats.text: Rama lay on a bed of sacred grass on the shore and prayed to Samudra, the ocean god, for three days and nights.
The sea did not answer. The waves rolled on as if Rama did not exist.

beats.visual: Rama's eyes turning red with anger
beats.text: On the fourth morning, Rama's eyes turned red. He reached for his bow.
In Lanka, Ravana's younger brother Vibhishana begged him: 'Return Sita and end this war. Bad omens are everywhere.'
The ministers laughed. Indrajit called him a coward.

beats.visual: Ravana kicking him from the throne
beats.text: Ravana kicked him out of the court in a rage. 'You are an enemy dressed as a brother.'

beats.visual: Vibhishana crossing the sky to Rama's camp
beats.text: Vibhishana flew across the sea with four loyal ministers to Rama's camp and asked for refuge.
Many advisors warned it was a trick. 'He is Ravana's brother,' Sugriva said. 'Kill him.'
Only Hanuman spoke for him. 'I have seen his heart. He is good.'
But Rama said, 'I never turn away someone who seeks shelter. Even if Ravana himself came to me, I would protect him.'
He crowned Vibhishana king of Lanka that day, with water from the sea.

title: Ram Setu
source: Valmiki, Yuddha Kanda 21-22 (the stones marked 'Ram' and the squirrel come from later retellings)

beats.visual: Rama raising his bow at the ocean
beats.text: When Samudra still did not appear, Rama raised his bow to dry up the sea. The waves boiled and sea creatures fled.
The ocean god rose from the waves with folded hands and begged for mercy. 'Build a bridge,' he advised. 'I will hold it.'

beats.visual: Nala and Neel directing the work
beats.text: He told Rama that the monkey Nala, son of the divine architect Vishwakarma, could build it. Nala and Neel guided the work.
Monkeys uprooted trees and broke off whole mountain peaks and threw them into the sea.
Later tellings say each stone was marked with Rama's name, and so it floated.

beats.visual: a small squirrel helping, Rama stroking it
beats.text: Even a little squirrel rolled in the sand and shook it onto the bridge. Rama stroked its back, and the three lines on squirrels, they say, are his fingers.

beats.visual: the army crossing the finished bridge
beats.text: In five days, the bridge to Lanka was ready, and the army crossed.

title: Angada's Mission
source: Valmiki, Yuddha Kanda 41 (the planted foot comes from later retellings)

beats.visual: Rama's army camped at Lanka's walls
beats.text: Rama's army camped at the gates of Lanka, and Rama looked up at the golden city where Sita was held.
Before war, Rama gave Ravana one last chance. He sent Prince Angada, Vali's son, as his messenger.
Angada walked into the demon king's court without fear, and stood before the ten-headed king.
Ravana mocked him. 'Your father was my friend. Why serve the man who killed him?'
'Return Sita,' Angada said. When the court laughed, he planted his foot and said, 'If any of you can move it, Rama will go home.'

beats.visual: warriors failing to lift his foot
beats.text: One by one, the mightiest demons strained and pulled. No one could move it.
Even Ravana rose to try. Angada stepped back. 'Do not touch my feet. Touch Rama's feet, and you will be saved.'

beats.visual: Angada leaping out of the palace
beats.text: Ravana did not listen. The last chance for peace was gone. Angada leapt through the palace roof and flew back to Rama.

beats.visual: two vast armies facing each other across Lanka's plain
beats.text: Rama's monkey army stood before Ravana's demon legions. Drums thundered. Conches roared across the plain.

beats.visual: Rama dividing his army at Lanka's four gates
beats.text: Rama divided his army to attack all four gates of Lanka at once. He took the north gate himself, where Ravana waited.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana at the front
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana led from the front. On the walls, Ravana watched with his ten heads, his twenty eyes burning.

beats.visual: demons pouring out of the gates
beats.text: The gates opened, and demons poured out on elephants and chariots, with swords, maces and spears.

beats.visual: boulders and trees hurled at the gates
beats.text: The monkeys charged with rocks, trees and bare hands, roaring Rama's name.
The battle raged all day. Blood ran like rivers. When night fell, the demons grew stronger, and still the monkeys fought on.

beats.visual: Hanuman and Angada fighting demon generals
beats.text: Demon generals fell one by one to Hanuman, Angada and Sugriva.
But Ravana's son Indrajit was yet to fight. Watching from the clouds, he smiled.

beats.visual: Indrajit hiding in the clouds, invisible
beats.text: Indrajit, master of illusion, fought from the clouds where no one could see him. He had once defeated Indra himself, and so got his name.

beats.visual: serpent arrows binding Rama and Lakshmana
beats.text: He shot the Nagapasha, arrows of living serpents, which bound both brothers from head to toe.
The brothers fell, covered in blood. The monkey army thought they were gone.
Indrajit rode back to Lanka and announced that Rama and Lakshmana were dead. Ravana laughed and celebrated.

beats.visual: Sita shown the fallen brothers from the flying chariot
beats.text: Ravana even sent Sita in his flying chariot to see them lying on the field. She wept, until Trijata whispered: 'Their faces still shine. They are alive.'
Sugriva and the monkeys wept around the brothers. Vibhishana tried to give them hope.
Then Garuda, the eagle king and enemy of serpents, swept in on a great wind. The snakes fled.
He touched their wounds, and they healed. The brothers rose, stronger than before, and the army roared.

title: Lakshmana Falls
source: Valmiki, Yuddha Kanda 101 (popular tellings give the spear to Indrajit)

beats.text: The fighting grew fiercer each day. Indrajit struck again and again, appearing and vanishing in the sky.
Lakshmana fought him arrow for arrow, protecting his brother's army.
At last a deadly Shakti spear was thrown at Lakshmana, blazing like lightning. Valmiki says Ravana threw it; many tellings say Indrajit.
Lakshmana fell, unconscious and barely breathing. The spear stuck deep in his chest.
Rama held him and wept. 'I can find another wife. I cannot find another brother.'
The whole army fell silent. Without Lakshmana, Rama said, he would not fight on.
The physician Sushena checked his pulse. 'He is alive. There is one hope: the Sanjeevani herb, from a mountain in the Himalayas.'
'But it must reach him before sunrise.' Every eye turned to Hanuman.

title: Sanjeevani
onscreen: A brother brought back from the edge.

beats.text: Sanjeevani grew on a faraway mountain in the Himalayas. Hanuman flew there in a single night, faster than the wind.
He crossed rivers, forests and kingdoms, until the white peaks of the Himalayas shone below him.

beats.visual: many glowing herbs on the peak
beats.text: But the mountain glowed with countless herbs, and he could not tell which was the right one. The herbs hid themselves from him.
So Hanuman lifted the whole mountain and carried it across the sky.

beats.visual: Hanuman carrying the mountain over the sea, moon behind
beats.text: He flew back over India and the sea, holding the glowing mountain in his hand like a lamp.

beats.visual: Lakshmana awakening as Sushena applies the herb
beats.text: Sushena found the herb, crushed it, and held it to Lakshmana's nose. Lakshmana opened his eyes just before dawn.
Rama embraced him, weeping with joy. The monkey army shouted until Lanka shook.
Then Hanuman carried the mountain back to where it belonged, before the sun rose.

beats.visual: Kumbhakarna asleep in a vast cave-palace
beats.text: Ravana's brother Kumbhakarna slept for six months at a time, by a boon gone wrong. He had meant to ask Brahma for Indra's throne, but his tongue slipped, and he asked for sleep.

beats.visual: demons waking him with drums and elephants
beats.text: The demons woke him with drums, conches and elephants marching over his body. They fed him mountains of food.
He told Ravana the truth: 'Sita's capture was wrong. Return her.'
But he still chose to fight for his brother. 'You are my king. I will die for you.'

beats.visual: the giant crushing the monkey army
beats.text: He was as tall as a mountain, and monkeys scattered in fear. He grabbed them by the handful and swallowed them. He even carried Sugriva away.
Then Rama faced him. His arrows cut off one arm, then the other, then his legs.
Rama's last arrow cut off his head. The giant fell into the sea, and the waves rose to the sky. He died with honor.

beats.visual: Indrajit performing a secret fire ritual
beats.text: Indrajit slipped away to perform a sacred ritual at the shrine of Nikumbhila. If he finished it, no one could ever defeat him.

beats.visual: Indrajit's illusion of Sita being killed
beats.text: To distract Rama, he first created an illusion of Sita and killed her before the monkeys' eyes. Rama fainted with grief.
Vibhishana rushed to him. 'It is a trick! Sita is safe. He is buying time for his ritual.'

beats.visual: Vibhishana pointing out the hidden place
beats.text: Vibhishana knew the secret and led Lakshmana to the ritual grounds.

beats.visual: Lakshmana attacking before the ritual ended
beats.text: Lakshmana broke the ritual and challenged Indrajit.

beats.visual: a fierce duel in the sky
beats.text: They fought for three days and nights. Arrows covered the sky like a storm.
At last Lakshmana took an arrow and swore: 'If Rama is truly devoted to dharma, let this arrow kill Indrajit.'
After a terrible fight, Lakshmana's arrow found its mark. Ravana's greatest warrior was no more.

beats.visual: Ravana in his golden chariot, eyes burning
beats.text: Mad with grief for his son, Ravana rode out himself in his golden chariot, his ten heads crowned and his twenty arms armed.
He scattered the monkey army like dry leaves in a storm.

beats.visual: Rama on foot against the demon king's chariot
beats.text: Rama had no chariot. So Indra sent his own divine chariot with its charioteer, Matali.

beats.visual: Indra's chariot descending from the sky
beats.text: It came down from heaven, drawn by green horses, shining like the sun.
For days they fought, arrow against arrow. The gods watched from the sky.

beats.visual: Rama cutting off Ravana's head, another growing
beats.text: Every time Rama cut off a head, another grew. A hundred heads fell, and a hundred grew back.

beats.visual: Agastya teaching Rama the Aditya Hridayam
beats.text: Then the sage Agastya appeared and taught Rama a sacred hymn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam, to give him strength.

beats.visual: Rama pausing, then rising with new strength
beats.text: Rama could not defeat Ravana by ordinary means. Only one weapon remained.

title: Ravana's End
source: Valmiki, Yuddha Kanda 108-111 (the nectar in the navel comes from later retellings; Valmiki says the arrow pierced his heart)

beats.text: Vibhishana whispered the secret: 'Ravana's life is hidden in the nectar in his navel.'

beats.visual: Matali reminding Rama of the Brahmastra
beats.text: Matali reminded Rama of the Brahmastra, the weapon of Brahma, given to Rama by Agastya.
Its feathers were the wind, its tip was fire and sun, and its weight was like the mountains Meru and Mandara.
Rama chanted a mantra and released it.
The arrow struck Ravana's navel. In Valmiki's telling, it pierced his heart. The mighty king of Lanka fell.
The gods showered flowers. The sun shone clear. The wind blew softly again over Lanka.
Even then, Rama asked Vibhishana to give his brother a proper funeral. 'Enmity ends with death,' he said. 'He is as much my brother now as yours.'
Vibhishana was crowned king of Lanka, as Rama had promised.

beats.visual: Sita walking out of the Ashok Vatika
beats.text: After the war, Hanuman brought word of victory to Sita. She was free at last. She could not speak for joy.

beats.visual: Sita bathed and dressed in a palanquin
beats.text: She was bathed, dressed in fine clothes and jewels, and brought to Rama in a palanquin.

beats.visual: Rama seeing Sita, silent and still
beats.text: When they met, Rama asked her to prove her purity before the world, for the sake of the people's trust.

beats.visual: Sita asking Lakshmana to build a pyre
beats.text: Sita, hurt but unbroken, asked Lakshmana to build a fire. 'If my heart has never left Rama, may Agni protect me.'
She walked around Rama, folded her hands, and stepped into the fire. Everyone cried out.

beats.visual: Agni, the fire god, lifting Sita unharmed
beats.text: Agni himself rose from the flames and returned her to Rama. Not a hair was burnt, not a flower in her garland faded. 'She is pure,' he said.
Rama took her hand. 'I knew it,' he said. 'But the world had to see it too.'

beats.visual: the flying Pushpak Vimana carrying Rama, Sita, Lakshmana
beats.text: The fourteen years of exile were ending. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana flew home in the Pushpak Vimana, with Hanuman, Sugriva and Vibhishana beside them.

beats.visual: Rama pointing out places below to Sita
beats.text: As they flew, Rama pointed down and showed Sita the bridge, Kishkindha, Panchavati, and Chitrakoot, where it had all begun.
Rama sent Hanuman ahead, so that Bharata would not enter the fire.
Bharata waited at the gates, holding the paduka, exactly as he had for fourteen years.
The brothers embraced, and the sandals were laid at Rama's feet.
Rama bowed to Kaushalya, Sumitra, and even Kaikeyi, with the same love.
That night, the whole city lit lamps to welcome their king home. We still celebrate that night as Diwali.
Rama was crowned king, and the golden age of Ram Rajya began.
